subject: frontend
question: Does this log [1, 2, 10]?
ai_claim: Yes. sort() puts the numbers in ascending order: 1, 2, 10.

ai_solution.text: scores contains 10, 1 and 2.
sort() orders the array in place.
The default order is ascending numeric order.
So it logs [1, 2, 10].

failure.explanation: Without a compare function, sort() converts elements to strings and compares them in UTF-16 order. '10' comes before '2' because '1' < '2', so the result is [1, 10, 2]. Use scores.sort((a, b) => a - b).
failure.why_convincing: With single-digit numbers the default sort happens to look numeric.

canonical_solution: It logs [1, 10, 2]: the default sort compares strings. Pass (a, b) => a - b.

hints.text: Check how sort() compares elements when no function is passed.
Step 3 states the default order.
The default comparison converts values to strings.
Compare '10' and '2' as strings.
Step 3 is wrong: the default sort is by string, giving [1, 10, 2]. Pass (a, b) => a - b.

debrief: JavaScript's default sort is lexicographic for every type. Always pass a compare function when sorting numbers, and test with multi-digit values.

subject: frontend
question: Does this log 0, 1 and 2?
ai_claim: Yes. Each timeout captures the value of i from its iteration, so the callbacks log 0, 1, 2.

ai_solution.text: The loop runs three times with i = 0, 1, 2.
Each iteration schedules a callback.
Each callback remembers i from its own iteration.
So it logs 0, 1, 2.

failure.misconception: Assuming var creates a new binding per iteration
failure.explanation: var is function-scoped, so all three callbacks close over the same variable i. The callbacks run after the loop finishes, when i is 3, so the output is 3, 3, 3. let creates a fresh binding for each iteration and would log 0, 1, 2.
failure.why_convincing: With let - the modern default - the claim would be exactly right.

canonical_solution: It logs 3, 3, 3: all callbacks share one var-scoped i, which is 3 when they run. Use let.

valid_evidence.summary: for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0); }

hints.text: Check when the callbacks run and what i is at that moment.
Step 3 claims each callback has its own i.
var is scoped to the function, not the loop body; closures capture variables, not values.
Find the value of i after the loop ends.
Step 3 is wrong: all callbacks share one i, which is 3 when they run. Use let.

debrief: Closures capture variables, not snapshots of values. With var there is one variable for the whole loop; with let there is one per iteration. Asynchronous callbacks make the difference visible.

subject: frontend
question: Does this run without error and log 'Ben'?
ai_claim: Yes. const prevents reassigning the variable user, not changing the object it refers to, so the property update works.

ai_solution.text: const makes the binding user permanent.
user.name = 'Ben' does not reassign user; it modifies the object.
Objects referenced by const variables remain mutable.
So it logs 'Ben'.

canonical_solution: Correct. const freezes the binding, not the value. Object.freeze(user) would be needed to prevent the property change.

valid_evidence.summary: user = {} would throw TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

hints.text: Separate reassigning the variable from changing the object.
Step 2 distinguishes the two operations.
const protects the binding; it does not make the object immutable.
Compare user.name = 'Ben' with user = {}.
This solution is correct. const prevents reassignment, not mutation, so it logs 'Ben'. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: const is about bindings: the variable always points to the same object, but that object can change. Immutability needs Object.freeze or immutable update patterns, as React state requires.

subject: frontend
question: Is it correct that isMissing returns true for null and undefined, and false for 0 and the empty string?
ai_claim: Yes. With ==, null equals only null and undefined, so the check catches both missing values without catching 0 or ''.

ai_solution.text: == performs type coercion for most comparisons.
But null == x is true only when x is null or undefined.
0 == null and '' == null are both false.
So isMissing returns true, true, false, false.

canonical_solution: Correct. value == null is the one widely accepted use of loose equality: it matches exactly null and undefined. (value ?? fallback relies on the same pair.)

valid_evidence.summary: isMissing(null), isMissing(undefined), isMissing(0), isMissing('') return true, true, false, false.
In the abstract equality algorithm, null and undefined are equal only to each other.

hints.text: Check the special rule for null in loose equality.
Step 2 states which values equal null.
Loose equality treats null and undefined as equal to each other and to nothing else.
Evaluate each of the four calls.
This solution is correct. value == null matches only null and undefined. The right judgment was to approve it.

debrief: Loose equality is usually avoided because its coercions surprise, but its null rule is simple and useful. Knowing exactly which values match is what makes it safe here.
